title: Rhythms of nature: how plants and birds keep time

summary.text: A bean plant lifts their leaves in the morning and lowers them at night, even inside a dark box. They keep time with a clock inside their body. Many living things have one. It runs on a rhythm of about 24 hours, and sunlight sets it right each morning. Flowers use their clocks to open when their visitors come: the lotus at dawn, jasmine in the evening, pavazhamalli at night. Over the year, living things also read the length of the day. Shorter days tell barn swallows to fly to India for the winter, and longer nights tell sevanthi plants to flower. So nature keeps a daily rhythm and a yearly rhythm, and living things get ready for each change before it comes.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left, a bean seedling on a windowsill at noon with leaves held flat, and at night with leaves hanging down. On the right, a line of swallows on an electric wire against a winter sky over a city.

intro.hook: Look at a bean plant at noon, and their leaves are spread out flat. Look again at bedtime, and the same leaves hang down. Put the plant in a dark box, where no light can reach. Will the leaves still lift in the morning? How could a plant know it is morning without seeing the sky?
intro.text: People have noticed these daily movements for thousands of years. Gardeners called them the 'sleep' of leaves. In this unit you grow a bean plant and test them yourself. You find out that living things carry a clock inside them. You also find out how birds know when to fly thousands of kilometres, and how flowers know when to open.
intro.art: A child kneeling by a windowsill, looking at a small bean seedling in a cup whose two leaves hang down in the evening light, with a cardboard box waiting beside the cup.

outcomes: I can say what a daily rhythm and a yearly rhythm are, with an example of each from plants, animals and people.
I can grow a bean plant, record their leaf positions through the day, and run a fair test with a dark box.
I can explain that many living things have a body clock that runs on about 24 hours and is set right by morning light.
I can explain why a plant, a flower or a bird is helped by getting ready before a change comes.
I can explain why birds migrate, and how the length of the day tells them when to go.
I can tell the true story of the stork with an arrow, and how it showed that birds fly south for the winter.
I can say what scientists agree on about body clocks and migration, and what they still do not know.

explanations.definition: A rhythm is a change that repeats at regular times. A daily rhythm repeats about every 24 hours. A yearly rhythm repeats about once a year.
explanations.description: The Earth spins once a day, so light and dark come round every 24 hours. The Earth also goes round the Sun once a year, so the seasons come round too. Almost every living thing changes with these two rhythms. Leaves droop at night. Flowers open at their own hour. Birds sing at dawn. In the year, trees flower, frogs call in the monsoon and birds come and go. People have daily rhythms too: sleeping, waking, feeling hungry.
examples: Every evening, house crows in Chennai fly to big trees to roost together.
Neem trees flower in March and April, near Ugadi. Neem flowers go into Ugadi pachadi.
Termites with wings fly out of the ground after the first big rains.
explanations.art: A big circle split into day and night, inside a bigger circle split into the seasons, with small pictures of a lotus, a bird and a sleeping child.
explanations.context: This card explains the two big rhythms of nature: the daily rhythm of light and dark, and the yearly rhythm of the seasons.

explanations.concept: The body clock inside living things
explanations.definition: A body clock is a timer inside a living thing. It keeps a rhythm of about 24 hours, even in steady darkness. Morning light sets it right each day.
explanations.description: A bean plant shut in a dark box still lifts their leaves in the morning and lowers them at night. Nothing outside tells them the time, so the timing must come from inside. Scientists call this a circadian rhythm. A body clock is not exact. In steady darkness it runs a little fast or a little slow, so it slowly drifts. Every morning, light resets it, the way you set a watch. The clock is made by genes and the substances they make. These build up and break down in a loop that takes about a day. In 2017, Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young won the Nobel Prize for finding this loop in fruit flies. Plants, fungi, many bacteria and people have clocks too.
examples: Your body is coolest in the early morning, before you wake, and warmest in the late afternoon.
A rooster often crows before the sky gets light.
In 1929, the Dutch botanist Anthonia Kleinhoonte showed that jack bean leaves kept moving up and down for days in steady darkness.
explanations.art: A bean seedling in a dark box with their leaves raised, and a faint dotted clock drawn inside their stem.
explanations.context: This card explains the body clock: the timer inside a living thing that keeps time without a window.

explanations.concept: Why it helps to be ready before sunrise
explanations.definition: A plant makes food from light, air and water. This is called photosynthesis. A body clock lets a plant prepare for light before the light arrives.
explanations.description: A plant's problem is that light comes for only part of the day, and every hour of it counts. If a plant waited for sunrise to start getting ready, they would waste part of the morning. With a clock, they lift their leaves and make the parts they need for photosynthesis before dawn. Then they can use the first light straight away. Scientists have tested this. Plants whose clock matched the length of the day grew bigger and made more food than plants whose clock did not match. Animals gain the same way. A bird that is awake and singing at first light is ready to feed as soon as insects move.
examples: A bean plant starts lifting their leaves before sunrise, while it is still dark.
In 2005, Antony Dodd and his team showed that plants with a matching clock grew better.
Many flowers make their scent at the hour their visitors come, and less at other times.
explanations.art: A bean plant raising their leaves in the dark blue light just before dawn, with the Sun still below the edge of the window.
explanations.context: This card explains why a body clock helps: being ready before a change comes saves time.

explanations.description: Bean, tamarind, touch-me-not and rain tree leaves all fold or droop at night. They move by a small joint, the pulvinus, at the base of each leaf. Water moves into the cells on one side of the joint and out of the other side, and the joint bends. Scientists agree on how the leaves move. They do not agree on why. Nobody has shown which answer is right for every plant.
examples: Rain trees on the roads of Bengaluru and Chennai fold their leaflets at night and on very cloudy days.
Tamarind leaflets fold together after sunset.
Touch-me-not folds at night and also when touched.

perspectives.explanation: Folded leaves lose less warmth to the cold night sky. He pinned some leaves open, and on cold nights those leaves were more often damaged by frost.
Folded leaves keep moonlight off their surface. Bright moonlight could confuse the plant's clock, which measures how long the night is.
Drooping leaves stay drier at night, so fewer fungi and germs grow on them. Or the leaves save water. These ideas are still being tested.

explanations.art: A rain tree at dusk with leaflets folded, and the same tree at noon with leaflets spread wide.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue over: why some plants fold or lower their leaves every night.

explanations.concept: Flowers that open at their own hour
explanations.definition: Many flowers open and close at about the same time each day. Their body clock and the light together set the time.
explanations.description: A flower's problem is that pollen must reach another flower of the same kind, and most flowers cannot move. So they need visitors, and visitors come at certain hours. Bees work in the day. Many moths fly at night. A flower open at the wrong hour wastes scent and nectar, and can be eaten by a hungry insect that does not carry pollen. So flowers open when their visitors are about. The lotus opens in the early morning and closes again later in the day, for about three days. Jasmine buds open in the evening. Pavazhamalli, the night jasmine, opens at night, and their flowers drop to the ground around dawn. White, sweet-smelling flowers that open at night are often visited by moths. In 1751, the Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus suggested a 'flower clock': a garden of flowers that open at different hours, so you could tell the time by looking.
examples: Malli buds bought in the afternoon open in the evening.
Four o'clock flowers open in the late afternoon. In Tamil they are called andhi mandharai, the evening flower.
Brahma kamal, called nishagandhi in Kerala, opens one night and fades by morning.
explanations.art: A round flower clock painted on paper, with a lotus at dawn, four o'clock flowers in the afternoon, jasmine in the evening and pavazhamalli at night.
explanations.context: This card explains why many flowers open at their own hour, and how that helps them.

explanations.definition: To migrate is to travel far, at the same time each year, and come back later. Birds migrate to find food and good places to raise their chicks.
explanations.description: A bird's problem in the far north is winter. Lakes freeze, snow covers the ground and insects disappear. A small bird must eat many times a day to stay warm, so staying would mean starving. So many birds fly south to warmer places, such as India, where there is food all winter. In spring they fly back north. There the summer days are very long, with lots of insects and space for nests. So they can feed their chicks for many hours each day. Barn swallows reach India from further north in the cold months, and line up on electric wires. Rosy starlings come from Central Asia and leave in spring. Amur falcons stop in Nagaland on their way from China and Siberia to southern Africa. Butterflies migrate too. In South India, huge numbers of blue tiger and crow butterflies travel between the plains and the Western Ghats each year.
examples: Barn swallows on the wires in winter, gone again by summer.
Lakhs of Amur falcons rest near the Doyang reservoir in Nagaland in October and November.
Arctic terns fly from the far north to Antarctica and back each year.
explanations.art: A map with arrows: swallows flying from the north into India, and Amur falcons flying from China through Nagaland and across the sea to Africa.
explanations.context: This card explains why birds make long journeys, starting with the problem winter gives them.

explanations.concept: How birds know when to go
explanations.definition: Birds tell the season mostly by day length. They also have a yearly clock inside them.
explanations.description: Day length changes the same way every year, so it is a safer signal than the weather. One warm week in winter does not change it. In birds, longer or shorter days change their hormones. Before a journey, they eat much more and store fat for fuel, and they become restless at night. Scientists have a German word for this restlessness, Zugunruhe. The German scientist Eberhard Gwinner kept warblers in a room where the light and warmth stayed the same all year. They still became restless and put on fat at about the times of their journeys. Their clock ran about 10 months instead of 12, so day length is needed to keep it on time. To find the way, birds use the Sun, the stars, the Earth's magnetic field, smells and landmarks.
examples: Before migrating, some small birds nearly double their weight with fat.
Many small birds migrate at night and rest and eat by day.
Young cuckoos fly to Africa alone, without ever having been there.
explanations.art: A small warbler in a cage at night, hopping and fluttering, facing the same direction as wild birds flying past outside.
explanations.context: This card explains how birds know when it is time to migrate, even inside a room with no windows.

explanations.concept: How plants tell the season: day length
explanations.definition: Photoperiodism is the way a plant or animal uses day length to tell the season.
explanations.description: Many plants flower only when the days reach a certain length. This lets all the plants of one kind flower together, so pollen can pass between them. In 1920, two American scientists, Wightman Garner and Harry Allard, found that one kind of tobacco plant flowered only when the days were short. They grew them in a shed and shortened the days by covering the plants, and they flowered. The plant is really measuring the length of the night. A flash of light in the middle of a long night can stop flowering. Farmers use this. Many rice varieties flower by day length. In Japan, some growers light chrysanthemum fields at night, so the plants flower later, when buyers want them.
examples: Sevanthi, the chrysanthemum, flowers when the nights grow long.
Many traditional rice varieties in India flower at about the same time of year, even when sown at different times.
Day length changes much more in Srinagar than in Chennai.
explanations.art: A plant under a box at evening, a farmer lifting the box at morning, and a calendar with the nights getting longer.
explanations.context: This card explains how plants use the length of the day to tell the season.

explanations.concept: Rhythms set by the Moon and the tides
explanations.definition: Some living things keep a rhythm with the Moon or the tides, as well as with the Sun.
explanations.description: The Moon goes from full moon to full moon in about 29 and a half days. The Moon's pull also makes the tides. Living things on the shore and in the sea have a problem: the water comes and goes, and sometimes they must all meet at once. On the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, many corals release their eggs on the same few nights after a full moon, once a year. So eggs from many corals meet in the water at the same time. In California, grunion fish come out of the sea onto beaches, just after the highest tides, to lay their eggs in wet sand. Crabs and other shore animals often move with the tides, about twice a day.
examples: Coral spawning on the Great Barrier Reef happens a few nights after a full moon in November or December.
Grunion lay eggs on Californian beaches after the highest spring tides.
Many crabs on Indian beaches come out at low tide.
explanations.art: Corals at night under a full moon, releasing tiny pink egg bundles that drift up like snow.
explanations.context: This card is about rhythms kept with the Moon and the tides, not only the Sun.

explanations.definition: A body clock works best when it matches the real day and the real year. Bright lights at night and a warming world can put rhythms out of step.
explanations.description: Most migrating birds fly at night. Bright lights on tall buildings can pull them off course. They circle the lights until they are tired, or fly into the glass. Some cities turn off building lights in the migration months to help them. In people, light from screens late at night can push the body clock later, so it is harder to fall asleep. As the world warms, some plants are flowering earlier in the year. In 2021, the cherry trees of Kyoto, in Japan, flowered at their earliest date in more than 1,200 years of records. If the flowers come early but their pollinators do not, both can go hungry.
examples: Chicago and New York ask tall buildings to dim their lights during the bird migration months.
Night-shift workers and people with jet lag feel tired at the wrong times.
Streetlights can make some birds sing in the middle of the night.
explanations.art: Small birds circling a brightly lit tower at night, while a dark building next to it has none around it.
explanations.context: This card is about what happens when a living thing's rhythm stops matching the real day or year.

agreed.text: Most living things have a body clock that keeps a rhythm of about 24 hours, even without light.
agreed.evidence: Plants, fungi, flies, mice and people kept in steady darkness keep a daily rhythm for days or weeks. Scientists have found the genes that make the clock.

agreed.text: Morning light resets the body clock each day.
agreed.evidence: Shift the times of light and dark, and the plant or animal shifts their rhythm within a few days. This is why jet lag wears off.

agreed.text: Many birds migrate each year to find food and places to raise chicks.
agreed.evidence: Rings on birds' legs since 1899, and now tiny trackers, show the same birds flying between the same places year after year.

agreed.text: Day length tells many plants and animals the season.
agreed.evidence: Change only the day length, keeping the warmth the same, and many plants flower and many birds get ready to migrate.

agreed.text: Leaves move by a joint at their base, called the pulvinus, where water moves in and out of cells.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the water and salts moving in the joint cells as the leaf rises and falls.

challenging.claim: Swallows spend the winter asleep in the mud at the bottom of ponds.
challenging.who: Many people in Europe for about 2,000 years, including the Greek thinker Aristotle and the Swedish writer Olaus Magnus in 1555
challenging.for: Swallows gather over ponds and reed beds in autumn, then suddenly vanish. Nobody had seen where they went.
challenging.against: No swallow was ever found alive in winter mud when people really looked. Rings and trackers show swallows flying to Africa and South Asia. The stork found in 1822 with an African spear in their neck had clearly been to Africa.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where birds go in winter.

challenging.claim: Some birds fly to the Moon for the winter.
challenging.who: An English teacher, Charles Morton, in a pamphlet written around 1700
challenging.for: Birds disappear high into the sky in autumn and return in spring. He worked out that a trip to the Moon could take about two months.
challenging.against: Space has no air to fly in. Trackers show the birds flying across the Earth, not up and away from it.
challenging.context: This card is about a strange old idea that was a real attempt to explain migration.

challenging.claim: Leaves fold at night only because it gets dark.
challenging.for: Leaves fold when it is dark, and darkness does make many leaves fold faster.
challenging.against: In a dark box, bean leaves still lift in the morning and lower in the evening, for several days. Their timing comes from a body clock inside them.
challenging.context: This card tests the idea that leaves simply react to darkness.

challenging.claim: Flowers open in the morning because the Sun warms them.
challenging.who: A common idea, and partly true
challenging.for: Some flowers, such as tulips and crocuses, open when they get warm and close when they cool down.
challenging.against: Many other flowers open at their hour even when the weather is cool or cloudy, because their clock times it. Jasmine opens in the evening, as it cools.
challenging.context: This card is about what really opens a flower: warmth, light or a clock.

challenging.claim: Birds migrate south because they feel cold.
challenging.for: Birds do leave as winter comes, and winter is cold.
challenging.against: Many birds leave while the weather is still warm, as the days shorten. Their real problem is food: frozen lakes and no insects. Birds with plenty of food in winter often stay.
challenging.context: This card asks whether cold itself, or the lack of food, sends birds away.

challenging.claim: Plants feel the time of day and decide when to move their leaves.
challenging.who: Plant scientists who study plant behaviour
challenging.for: Plants sense light, darkness and the length of the night. They measure time and act before the change comes, which is what deciding looks like in any living thing.
challenging.against: Some scientists call these automatic responses run by genes, with no thinking involved.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the word 'decide' fits what a plant does.

big_questions.q: Your bean plant lifted their leaves before any light reached them. How could they know morning was coming?
big_questions.hint: Think about what had happened to the plant on all the days before the box.

big_questions.q: A body clock runs a little too fast or too slow. Why would a living thing need light every morning to set it right?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a watch that gains five minutes a day, if nobody ever sets it?

big_questions.q: A swallow that spends half the year in Russia and half in India: which place is their home?
big_questions.hint: Where do they raise chicks? Where do they spend most days? Can a home be two places?

big_questions.q: Why might day length be a better signal of the season than warmth?
big_questions.hint: Can one hot week in January change the day length?

big_questions.q: Plants, birds and people all keep time. Is time something in the world, or something living things make?
big_questions.hint: The Earth spins whether anyone is watching. A clock is something a body builds. Is a day the same thing for a bean and for you?

big_questions.q: Electric light lets people stay awake long after sunset. What do we gain, and what might we lose?
big_questions.hint: Think of sleep, of birds flying at night, and of moths around a lamp.

story.title: Paati's Balcony Calendar
story.note: Arjun, Paati and their flat are made up. The nature is true: pavazhamalli flowers open at night and fall around dawn, mostly from about August to December. Barn swallows spend the cold months in India. Sevanthi flowers as the nights grow long. Neem flowers around Ugadi. Winged termites fly out after the first heavy rains.
text: Arjun was eight when he and his mother moved into Paati's flat in Mysuru. It was on the fourth floor, with a narrow balcony full of pots. There was a big calendar on the kitchen wall, with a picture of Chamundi Hill. Paati never looked at it.
'How do you know what month it is?' Arjun asked her.
'The balcony tells me,' said Paati. She was watering her sevanthi plants, which had no flowers at all.
Arjun laughed. 'A balcony can't tell you the month.'
'Then catch me out,' said Paati. 'Write down everything the balcony shows you, for one whole year. If I'm wrong even once, I'll make you payasam every Sunday.'
So Arjun got a notebook. On the first page he wrote 'Paati's Mistakes', and underlined it twice.

In August, Paati said, 'The pavazhamalli tree by the temple wall will start dropping flowers soon.' Arjun went down for the milk packets at half past six every morning. For a week, the ground under the tree was bare. Then one morning it was white. Hundreds of small white flowers with orange stems lay on the ground, and they smelled sweet. He looked up. There were new buds on the tree, but no open flowers.
'They open at night,' said Paati, 'and fall at dawn. Every night, the same.' Arjun wrote it down, under 'Things Paati Got Right'. He had not planned to have that page.

He tested it. He went down earlier, at six. The flowers were still falling, one by one, like slow snow. He went down at nine in the evening with a torch. The tree was covered in open flowers, and the whole lane smelled of them. In the morning they were on the ground again.

In October, Paati said, 'The swallows will come to the wires.' A week later, Arjun saw them: small dark birds with long forked tails and red throats, sitting in a neat row on the electric wire. In the evening there were thirty. He counted twice.
'Where were they before?' he asked.
'Far to the north,' said Paati. 'Where it's getting cold now, and the insects are going. They come here, where there is food all winter.'
'But how do they know it's October? They don't have a calendar either.'
Paati smiled. 'Watch the evenings,' she said. 'You tell me.'

So Arjun wrote down the time the streetlights came on. In June they had come on at about seven. Now they came on before six. The days were getting shorter. He did not know yet how a swallow could tell. But he could see that something in the sky was changing, and it changed the same way every year.
In December, the nights were long and cool. The sevanthi plants, which had been green leaves for months, grew tight little buds. By the end of the month the balcony was yellow.
'They wait for the long nights,' said Paati. 'Then they know.'

In March, Paati said, 'The neem is flowering. Ugadi is coming.' The neem tree outside the gate was covered in tiny white flowers, and bees buzzed round it all day. Paati picked some and made Ugadi pachadi, sweet and sour and bitter all at once. In April, the swallows were gone from the wires. Arjun's 'Paati's Mistakes' page was still empty.
Then, in May, Arjun had his chance. 'Paati, when do the eesal come out?' he asked. Eesal were winged termites. Every year they flew out of the ground in clouds and danced round the streetlights.
'After the first big rain,' said Paati.

Last year, the first big rain had come in early May. This year, May was dry and hot. The ground cracked. No eesal came. On the last day of May, Arjun opened his notebook to 'Paati's Mistakes' and picked up his pencil.
'Wait,' said Paati. 'Did I say May?'
Arjun stopped. She had not. She had said, 'After the first big rain.'

The rain came on the ninth of June. It poured for an hour, and the road turned to a river. That evening, as the streetlight came on, the air filled with thousands of fluttering wings. Arjun and Paati stood on the balcony and watched them, whirling in the light.

That night, Arjun read his whole notebook from the start. The pavazhamalli opened every night at the same time. The swallows came as the evenings grew short. The sevanthi flowered when the nights grew long. Those things kept to the light, and the light kept to the year. But the eesal had waited for the rain, and the rain was different every year.
'The calendar on the wall counts days,' said Paati. 'The balcony counts light, and rain.'
Arjun turned to the empty page and crossed out 'Paati's Mistakes'. Above it he wrote 'Arjun's Nature Calendar'. Then he went to the kitchen. 'Paati,' he said, 'can we make payasam anyway?'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Paati's signs come in two kinds. Some follow the light: flowers that open at the same hour each night, swallows that arrive as the days shorten, sevanthi that flowers when the nights grow long. Day length changes the same way every year, so these signs are very steady. Other signs follow the weather, like winged termites after the first heavy rain, so they come on a different date each year. Arjun thought Paati was reading the calendar. She was really reading the same signals the living things read.
ask: How did Arjun find out when the pavazhamalli flowers open and fall?
What did Arjun notice about the streetlights, and how might that help a swallow know the season?
Why did the eesal come out in June this year, when last year they came out in May?
Which of Paati's signs were the most steady from year to year, and why?
Arjun started his notebook to catch Paati out. What did he end up with instead? Have you ever set out to prove someone wrong and learned something else?

rules: Shuffle the cards. Each player takes 5 cards.
On your turn, put one card on the part of the clock where you think it belongs, and say why.
The other players check the answer in the brackets. Right, and you keep the card as a point. Wrong, and it goes to the bottom of the pile.
Playing alone, place all 20 cards, then check them and count your points.
When all cards are placed, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and lay out the clock board. 2. Deal 5 cards to each player.
flow.say: Every living thing has their own time to be busy. Let's see if you know when.
flow.kid: Lay out the clock. Take 5 cards. Each card is a living thing. Where on the clock do they go?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Nature's Clock card game. You set up the clock board and the cards.

flow.do: Play the practice card 'Fruit bats flying out'.
flow.say: Practice card: fruit bats flying out. Dawn, day, dusk or night?
flow.kid: Practice card. Fruit bats flying out. When does this happen? Tap your answer.

check.q: When do fruit bats fly out of their trees to eat?
check.why: Fruit bats rest hanging in big trees all day and fly out at dusk to find fruit. They are nocturnal. 'Night' is close, because they eat all night, but they set out at dusk.

flow.do: Take turns placing cards and saying why.
flow.say: Place a card and give a reason. Why do they go there?
flow.kid: Place a card. Say why. Check the answer.

flow.do: Count the points and look at the finished clock.
flow.say: Look at our clock. Is any part of the day empty?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at the clock. Is any time empty?
flow.think: If every time of day has someone busy, is there ever a quiet moment in nature?

games.title: Falcon Flight: Nagaland to Africa
games.context: This is a board game about the migration of Amur falcons. Players fly from China to Nagaland and across the sea to Africa, answering questions about rhythms of nature.

printables.title: A journey board of 24 squares
items: Square 0: Eastern China, the start. Days are getting shorter.
Squares 3 and 10: STORM. Miss a turn.
Square 8: Doyang reservoir, Nagaland. REST AND EAT: roll again.
Squares 12 to 20: THE SEA. No resting here. Answer wrong, and go back 2.
Square 16: BRIGHT LIGHTS on a ship. Go back 1, unless you can say why lights are a problem for migrating birds.

printables.title: 20 question cards
items: What does 'migrate' mean? (To travel far at the same time each year, and come back)
Why do falcons leave the north in autumn? (Food runs out in winter)
What tells many birds it is time to go? (The days getting shorter)
What is a body clock? (A timer inside a living thing, about 24 hours long)
What resets the body clock each morning? (Light)
Name a flower that opens at night. (Pavazhamalli, or Brahma kamal)
Name a flower that opens in the morning. (Lotus)
When do jasmine buds open? (In the evening)
What do bean leaves do at night? (Hang down)
Do bean leaves still lift in the morning inside a dark box? (Yes)
What did people once think swallows did in winter? (Slept in mud under lakes)
What did the stork found in 1822 have in their neck? (A spear from Africa)
Who are pollinators? (Animals that carry pollen between flowers)
When is your body coolest? (In the early morning)
What do birds store before a long flight? (Fat)
What is the restlessness of caged birds at migration time called? (Zugunruhe)
Name a butterfly that migrates in South India. (Blue tiger)
What does the Moon set the time for on coral reefs? (When corals release their eggs)
Which plant flowers when the nights grow long? (Sevanthi)
Why do lights on tall buildings harm migrating birds? (Birds fly towards them and can crash or tire)

printables.title: One paper falcon for each player

rules: On your turn, another player reads you a question card. Playing alone, read it yourself and check the answer in the brackets.
Answer right, and roll the dice and move. Answer wrong, and move 1 square.
Follow what the square says. On the SEA squares, a wrong answer sends you back 2, because there is nowhere to rest.
The first falcon to reach southern Africa wins. Playing alone, try to finish in 12 turns or fewer.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Put the falcons on square 0. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: Amur falcons fly from China to Nagaland, rest and eat, then cross the sea to Africa. Let's fly with them.
flow.kid: Put your falcon on the start. You are flying to Africa. Rest in Nagaland. Then cross the sea!
flow.context: This is the first step of Falcon Flight, a board game about the Amur falcon's migration.

flow.do: Play one practice card together.
flow.say: Practice card. What tells many birds it is time to go?
flow.kid: Practice card. What tells birds it is time to go? Tap your answer.

check.q: What tells many birds it is time to migrate?
check.why: Day length changes the same way every year, so it is a steady signal. 'Other birds telling them' is a fair idea, because birds often fly in flocks. But young birds of some kinds migrate alone, at the right time, without being shown.

flow.do: Take turns until a falcon reaches Africa.
flow.say: Answer, roll and fly. Careful over the sea.
flow.kid: Answer. Roll. Fly! Be careful over the sea.

flow.do: Talk about the sea squares.
flow.say: Real Amur falcons cross the sea for days without landing. How do you think they get ready for that?
flow.kid: Real falcons fly over the sea for days without stopping. How do they get ready?
flow.think: What would you need to carry for a trip with nowhere to stop?

experiments.title: Sleeping Bean Leaves: do they need to see the morning?
experiments.question: A bean plant lifts their leaves in the day and lowers them at night. If we shut the plant in a dark box, will the leaves still lift in the morning?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the bean leaves in the dark box stay down all the time, stay up all the time, or still go up in the morning and down at night? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Grow two cups of bean plants from the same packet, in the same soil, with the same water, on the same windowsill. On the test day, only one thing changes: one cup goes into a dark box, and the other stays by the window. Both stay in the same room, so they are equally warm. Check both cups at the same times. Peek into the box quickly, for a few seconds, so very little light gets in.
results_table: Window cup: flat, half down or hanging down?
Box cup: flat, half down or hanging down?

materials.item: 6 dry rajma (kidney bean) seeds from the kitchen
2 paper or plastic cups, or two plastic bottles cut to cup size, each with 2 small holes poked in the bottom
soil from a potted plant, or a small bag of potting soil. Damp cotton wool also works for the first two weeks.
a cardboard box big enough to cover one cup, such as a shoebox, with its gaps taped
a sheet of paper, to make a leaf position card
a small plate under each cup, to catch water

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes in the cups. Wash hands after handling soil. Raw rajma seeds must not be eaten.

schedule.what: Soak 6 rajma seeds in water overnight.
Plant 3 seeds in each cup and put both cups on a bright windowsill.
Water a little if the soil feels dry. Do this every day until the test.
When the first two leaves are open, check both cups at 7 in the morning, 1 in the afternoon, 6 in the evening and 9 at night. At 6 in the evening, after the check, put one cup into the dark box.
Check both cups at 7 in the morning, 1 in the afternoon and 9 at night. Peek into the box quickly.
Check both cups at 7 in the morning. Then take the box cup out and put it back by the window.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at every check. Draw the leaves of both cups at 7 in the morning on day 11. Then write what you think, what you saw and why.

flow.do: 1. Put 6 rajma seeds in a bowl. 2. Cover them with water. 3. Leave them overnight.
flow.say: We are going to grow bean plants. Their leaves move, and we will test why. Soaking wakes the seeds up.
flow.kid: Put 6 rajma seeds in a bowl of water. Leave them overnight. Soaking wakes the seeds up.
flow.parent: Kitchen rajma usually sprouts. Older seeds may not, which is why we plant 6. If none sprout in a week, try fresh rajma, or ask a nursery for bean seeds.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sleeping bean leaves experiment. It takes about 12 days, because the beans need to grow first.

flow.do: 1. Poke 2 small holes in the bottom of each cup. 2. Fill both cups with soil. 3. Push 3 soaked seeds into each cup, a finger-joint deep. 4. Water gently and put both cups on plates on a bright windowsill.
flow.say: Both cups get the same seeds, soil, water and window. Then the only difference later will be the one we choose.
flow.kid: Fill both cups with soil. Push 3 seeds into each, a finger-joint deep. Water them. Put them by a bright window.
flow.parent: Poke the holes yourself with a skewer or a hot needle held in tongs. The holes let extra water drain away, so the roots do not rot.
flow.wait: Water a little each day if the soil feels dry. The shoots come up in about 4 to 7 days.

flow.do: 1. When the first two leaves have opened, make a leaf position card. 2. On a sheet of paper, draw three bean leaves on a stalk: one flat, one half down and one hanging down. 3. Label them.
flow.say: This card helps us describe what the leaves are doing, so we write it the same way each time.
flow.kid: Draw three leaves on a stalk. One flat. One half down. One hanging down. Label them. This is your leaf position card.
flow.parent: The first two leaves of a bean are single, heart-shaped leaves, opposite each other. They usually open about 8 to 12 days after planting. Wait for them before starting the checks.
flow.wait: Start the checks on the first day both cups have open leaves.

flow.do: 1. Check both cups at 7 in the morning, 1 in the afternoon, 6 in the evening and 9 at night. 2. Each time, hold the leaf position card beside a leaf. 3. Write flat, half down or hanging down in the table.
flow.say: Let's watch the leaves through one whole day. What do they do at night?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves four times today. Morning, afternoon, evening and night. Are they flat, half down or hanging down? Write it down.

ask.q: What did the leaves do between the evening and night checks?
good: They were hanging down at night, but flat in the day.

flow.parent: In the day the leaves are held out flat. By night they usually droop until they hang almost straight down. If your room is lit late at night, check in a dim corner, or turn the room light off for the night check.

flow.do: 1. At 6 in the evening, after the check, put one cup on its plate in a corner of the same room. 2. Cover it with the box. 3. Make sure no light gets in at the edges.
flow.say: Now the test. This cup will not see the night end, or the morning come. Before we close it, what do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Put one cup in the corner. Cover it with the box. No light can get in now. What will the leaves do in the morning? Guess, and say why.

check.q: Why do we put the box cup in the same room as the window cup?
options: So the box cup can see the window
So both cups stay equally warm, and only the light is different
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the box cup were in a cooler room, we could not tell whether the dark or the cold made any difference. Picking 'so we don't forget it' is sensible, but it is not why it makes the test fair.

flow.do: 1. At 7 the next morning, look at the window cup. 2. Then lift the box for 5 seconds, look at the box cup and cover it again. 3. Write both in the table. 4. Do the same at 1 in the afternoon and 9 at night.
flow.say: Quickly, before much light gets in. Are the box leaves up or down?
flow.kid: Look at the window cup. Now lift the box and peek, very quickly. Are the leaves up or down? Cover it again. Write it down.

check.q: The box cup has had no light since last evening. In the morning, their leaves are flat again. What does this show?
options: The plant has a clock inside them that tells them it is morning
The leaves are tired of hanging down
check.why: No light reached the plant, yet their leaves rose at about the right time. So the timing must come from inside them. This is called a body clock. Picking 'light got in' is a good scientist's doubt. Check your box for gaps, and look again at 9 at night: the leaves should go down in the dark too.

flow.parent: Expect the box leaves to rise in the morning and fall again at night, though often a little less far than the window leaves. If the box leaves stayed down all day, check that the plants are healthy and the soil is damp, and try again with the other cup.

flow.do: 1. On the next morning, check both cups once more. 2. Take the box away and put the box cup back by the window.
flow.say: Two mornings in the dark. Did the leaves still know? Now the plant can have their light back.
flow.kid: Check both cups one more time. Then take the box off. Put the cup back by the window.
flow.parent: A plant can keep this rhythm for several days in darkness, but they cannot make food without light. One or two days in the dark does no harm.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the bean plant has a clock inside them. What I saw: in the dark box, the leaves were flat in the morning and hanging down at night, like the window cup. Why: no light reached them, so the timing came from inside the plant. The days on the windowsill had set their clock.

experiments.context: In this experiment you grow bean plants and watch their leaves move through the day. Then you shut one plant in a dark box, to find out whether the leaves need light to know when it is morning.

experiments.title: Warm and Cool: does your body keep a daily rhythm?
experiments.question: Is your body the same warmth all day, or does it change at the same times each day?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When will your body be warmest: just after waking, in the late afternoon, or at bedtime? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same digital thermometer, in the same place on your body, each time. Measure after sitting still for 15 minutes, not after running, a bath or a hot meal. Measure at the same three times on three days, because one reading can be a fluke.

materials.item: a digital thermometer, the kind used for fevers
a notebook and pencil, kept by the bed
a clock or phone, to note the time

experiments.safety: Use only a digital thermometer. Never use an old glass thermometer, because it can break, and some have mercury inside. Wipe the thermometer clean before and after each use.

schedule.what: Measure your temperature just after waking, at about 5 in the afternoon and at bedtime.
Measure again at the same three times.
Measure again at the same three times. Then work out which time was warmest on most days.

experiments.record: Write each temperature in the table, to one decimal place, for example 36.4. At the end, circle the warmest reading of each day.

flow.do: 1. Keep the thermometer and notebook by the bed. 2. As soon as your child wakes, before getting up, measure their temperature.
flow.say: Before you get up or eat anything, let's measure how warm your body is. We'll measure the same way three times a day.
flow.kid: Don't get up yet. Put the thermometer in place. Wait for the beep. Write the number down.
flow.parent: Use the same place each time: under the tongue if your thermometer is made for the mouth, or deep in the armpit with the arm held close. A healthy reading is usually between about 36 and 37.5 °C. If your child has a fever or a cold, wait until they are well.
flow.context: This is the first step of the warm and cool experiment. You measure your body's temperature three times a day, for three days, to look for a rhythm.

flow.do: 1. At about 5 in the afternoon, ask your child to sit still for 15 minutes, reading or drawing. 2. Then measure in the same place.
flow.say: Sitting still first matters, because running about makes your body warmer for a while.
flow.kid: Sit quietly for 15 minutes. Then measure again, in the same place. Write it down.

flow.do: 1. At bedtime, after brushing teeth, measure once more. 2. Do all three measurements again on day 2 and day 3.
flow.say: Last one for today. Do you think it will be higher or lower than this morning?
flow.kid: Measure once more at bedtime. Guess first: higher or lower than this morning?
flow.wait: Measure at the same three times tomorrow and the day after.

flow.do: 1. Look at all nine readings together. 2. Circle the warmest reading of each day. 3. Work out the difference between the morning and the afternoon readings on each day.
flow.say: Was the warmest time the same on most days? How big was the difference?
flow.kid: Circle the warmest number of each day. Was it the same time of day each time?

check.q: On most days, Kavya's temperature was lowest just after waking and highest in the late afternoon. What does this show?
options: Her body warms and cools on a daily rhythm
She had a fever every afternoon
check.why: In most people, the body is coolest in the early morning and warmest in the late afternoon or evening, by about half a degree. The body clock runs this rhythm. A fever is much bigger, usually above 38 °C. Picking 'broken thermometer' is a fair doubt, which is why we measured on three days.

flow.parent: Most people find their morning reading lowest and their late afternoon or evening reading highest, by about 0.3 to 0.6 °C. Underarm readings jump about more. If your numbers show no pattern, that is real data too. Talk about what could have made the readings jump.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: my body has a daily rhythm of warmth. What I saw: on two of three days, I was coolest just after waking and warmest at 5 pm. Why: my body clock warms my body in the day, when I am active, and cools it at night for sleep.

experiments.context: In this experiment you measure your own body's warmth at three times of day, for three days, to find out whether your body keeps a daily rhythm.

experiments.title: Malli Buds: when do jasmine flowers open?
experiments.question: Jasmine buds open in the evening. Do they need to see the evening come, or will they open on time in the dark?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the buds kept in a closed dabba open at the same time as the buds on an open plate, later, or not at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use 20 buds from the same string or bunch. Put 10 on a damp cloth on an open plate, and 10 on a damp cloth inside a closed steel dabba, next to each other in the same room. Only the light is different. Count the open buds at the same times.

materials.item: about 20 malli (jasmine) buds, bought loose or on a string in the afternoon. Buds from a jasmine plant in a pot also work.
2 small cloths or kerchiefs, dampened
a plate, and a steel dabba with a lid big enough to hold 10 buds

experiments.safety: None needed. Wash the buds' cloths afterwards.

schedule.what: In the afternoon, set up the plate and the dabba. Count open buds at 4 pm, 6 pm, 8 pm and 10 pm.
Count once more in the morning, and see what the open flowers look like now.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each check. Draw one bud at 4 pm and the same flower at 10 pm.

flow.do: 1. Buy jasmine buds in the afternoon, closed and white or pale green. 2. Count 20 buds. 3. Lay 10 on a damp cloth on a plate. 4. Lay 10 on a damp cloth in a steel dabba and close the lid. 5. Put both side by side on a table.
flow.say: Flower sellers sell jasmine as buds in the afternoon. Let's find out exactly when they open, and whether they need light to do it.
flow.kid: Count 20 buds. Put 10 on a damp cloth on a plate. Put 10 in the dabba and close the lid. Put them side by side.
flow.parent: Choose buds that are still tightly closed. Fully open flowers in the afternoon will spoil the count.
flow.context: This is the first step of the malli buds experiment. You watch jasmine buds through one evening, to see when they open and whether darkness changes it.

flow.do: 1. At 4, 6, 8 and 10 in the evening, count the open buds on the plate. 2. Open the dabba, count quickly, and close it again. 3. Smell both and write how strong the smell is.
flow.say: How many are open now? Can you smell them yet?
flow.kid: Count the open flowers on the plate. Peek in the dabba and count. Close it fast. Smell them. Write it all down.

ask.q: When did most of the buds open?

flow.parent: Most jasmine buds open in the evening, and the smell gets much stronger at night. We could not find a study on whether buds in darkness open at the same time, so your result is real new data. Either answer teaches something.

flow.do: Next morning, look at the flowers on the plate and in the dabba.
flow.say: What do the flowers look like this morning? Do they still smell?
flow.kid: Look at yesterday's flowers. Are they still fresh? Do they still smell?

check.q: Why might it help a jasmine flower to open and smell strongest in the evening?
options: Their visitors, such as moths, come at that time
The flower is afraid of the Sun
Evening air is heavier and holds petals open
check.why: A flower must get pollen to another flower, and visitors carry it. Many white, sweet-smelling flowers that open at evening are visited by moths, which fly at night. Opening at the right hour saves scent for when it is needed. 'Afraid of the Sun' is a guess about feelings, but the experiment cannot test it.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer gives the times. For example: by 4 pm no buds were open, by 8 pm seven of ten on the plate were open. Then it compares the dabba. If the dabba buds opened on time too, the timing came from inside the buds. If they opened later or less, the evening light may matter. Both are honest results.

experiments.context: In this experiment you watch jasmine buds through one evening, to find out when they open and whether they need light to open on time.

activities.title: What Time Is It? Clues without a clock

materials.item: a window, and paper and pencil

activities.safety: Stay inside the window grille or balcony rail.

schedule.what: Cover the clocks, find clues to the time of day, then guess it.

activities.record: List your clues. Put a star next to the clues that come from living things.

flow.do: 1. Turn the clocks away and put phones face down. 2. Stand at a window with your child for 3 minutes. 3. Ask them to find every clue to the time of day: light, shadows, sounds, smells, how they feel.
flow.say: No clocks for a few minutes. What can you see, hear, smell or feel that tells you what time of day it is?
flow.kid: No clocks! Look out of the window. Listen. Sniff. How do you feel? Find clues to the time.

ask.q: Which clues come from living things?
good: I'm hungry, so it's nearly lunch.
The flower seller has jasmine buds.

flow.context: This is the first step of a short noticing activity. You find clues to the time of day without looking at a clock.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess the time. 2. Turn a clock round and check.
flow.say: So what time do you think it is? Let's check.
flow.kid: Guess the time. Now check the clock. How close were you?

flow.do: Look at the clues that came from living things, and ask the question for the unit.
flow.say: Your tummy knew it was nearly lunch. The crows knew it was evening. None of them looked at a clock. So how do living things know the time?
flow.kid: Your tummy and the crows knew the time. They have no clock to look at. How do they know?
flow.think: Could a plant know the time? How could we test it?

activities.context: This short noticing activity opens the unit. You find clues to the time of day, and notice that many come from living things that have no clock.

setup.caption: 1. Hide the clocks. Find clues at the window.

activities.title: Make a Flower Clock

materials.item: a paper plate or a circle of card
colour pencils or crayons
a split pin or a pin and an eraser, and a paper arrow

activities.safety: A grown-up pushes the pin through the plate.

schedule.what: Draw a clock with flowers placed at the hours they open, and add a turning arrow.

activities.record: Your flower clock. On the back, write one flower you can check for yourself.

flow.do: 1. Read your child this list. Lotus opens in the early morning. Four o'clock flowers open in the late afternoon. Jasmine opens in the evening. Pavazhamalli opens at night and falls at dawn. Brahma kamal opens late at night.
flow.say: In 1751, a Swedish botanist called Carl Linnaeus had an idea. He said you could tell the time by which flowers were open. Let's make one.
flow.kid: Some flowers open at their own hour. Lotus in the morning. Jasmine in the evening. Let's make a clock of flowers.
flow.context: This is the first step of making a flower clock. Some flowers open at about the same hour each day, so a clock can be made from them.

flow.do: 1. Draw a big circle and split it into day and night. 2. Draw each flower at the time it opens. 3. Add a sun at the top of the day side and a moon on the night side.
flow.say: Put the lotus near sunrise and the jasmine at evening. Where does the pavazhamalli go?
flow.kid: Draw each flower at its time. Lotus near sunrise. Jasmine in the evening. Where does pavazhamalli go?

flow.do: 1. Push the pin through a paper arrow and the middle of the plate. 2. Ask your child to turn the arrow to now, and say which flowers would be open.
flow.say: Turn the arrow to now. Which flowers would be open?
flow.kid: Turn the arrow to now. Which flowers are open right now?

check.q: Why do different flowers open at different hours?
options: The Sun reaches each flower at a different time
They take turns, to be fair
Each opens when their visitors, such as bees or moths, are about
check.why: Flowers need visitors to carry their pollen. Bees fly by day, and many moths at night. A flower that opens when their visitors come wastes less scent and nectar. 'The Sun reaches each flower at a different time' is not right: in one garden, the Sun rises for every flower at once.

activities.context: In this activity you make a flower clock, showing which flowers open at which hour, as Carl Linnaeus suggested in 1751.

activities.title: Morning People and Night People: a family survey

materials.item: paper and pencil
family members, or relatives on the phone

schedule.what: Ask family members four questions about when they feel most awake, and compare the answers by age.

activities.record: A table with each person's age, when they wake on a holiday, and when they feel most awake.

flow.do: 1. Help your child draw a table with four columns: name, age, 'wakes on a holiday at', 'feels most awake at'. 2. Fill it in for your child first.
flow.say: Every person has a body clock, but not all clocks are set the same. Let's find out who in our family is a morning person.
flow.kid: Make a table. Name, age, wakes on a holiday at, feels most awake at. Fill in your own row first.
flow.context: This is the first step of a family survey about body clocks. You ask people when they feel most awake.

flow.do: 1. Ask at least three people of different ages, such as a grandparent, a parent and a cousin. 2. Write their answers in the table.
flow.say: Ask each person: when do you wake up on a holiday, with no alarm? When do you feel most awake?
flow.kid: Ask each person two questions. When do you wake on a holiday? When do you feel most awake? Write it down.

flow.do: Look at the table together, ordered by age.
flow.say: Do the older people wake earlier? What about any teenagers?
flow.kid: Put the people in order of age. Who wakes earliest? Who wakes latest?

check.q: Scientists have found that most teenagers' body clocks run later than younger children's and grandparents'. What would that look like?
options: Teenagers feel sleepy later at night, and find early mornings hard
check.why: Body clocks shift with age. Young children and older people tend to wake early. Teenagers' clocks run later, so they feel awake late at night and sleepy in the morning. It is not laziness. 'No sleep' is wrong: teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours.

flow.parent: Small families give small numbers, so this shows a pattern only roughly. That is fine. The point is that body clocks differ between people, and change with age.

activities.context: In this activity you survey your family to find out who is a morning person and who is a night person, and whether it changes with age.

activities.title: Map the Journeys

materials.item: a printed world map, or one drawn from an atlas
three colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw the journeys of three migrating animals on a world map.

activities.record: Your map, with a key for the three colours and the months of each journey.

flow.do: 1. In red, draw the Amur falcon's journey. Start in eastern Russia and China. 2. Draw the arrow to Nagaland, in north-east India, for October. 3. Carry it on across the Arabian Sea to southern Africa. 4. Draw a dotted arrow back for spring.
flow.say: Amur falcons are small falcons. They rest in Nagaland in October, then fly about 4,000 kilometres over the sea to Africa.
flow.kid: Draw the Amur falcon's journey in red. From China, to Nagaland, over the sea to Africa. Then a dotted line back.
flow.context: This is the first step of mapping three animal journeys. Each journey happens at the same time every year.

flow.do: 1. In blue, draw an arrow for barn swallows, from Central Asia and Russia down to India. 2. They come for the cold months and go back in spring.
flow.say: The barn swallows on the wires in winter came from far to the north. Where do they go in summer?
flow.kid: Draw the barn swallow in blue. From the far north, down to India for winter. Then back.

flow.do: 1. In green, draw a short arrow inside South India, for blue tiger and crow butterflies. 2. Draw it between the plains and the Western Ghats.
flow.say: Butterflies migrate too. In South India, huge numbers of blue tiger butterflies travel between the plains and the Western Ghats.
flow.kid: Draw the blue tiger butterfly in green. A short trip, inside South India.

flow.do: Talk about what the three journeys have in common.
flow.say: All three journeys come at the same time every year. What tells them when?
flow.kid: All three go at the same time every year. What tells them when to go?

check.q: What tells many migrating birds when to start their journey?
check.why: Day length changes the same way every year, so it is a steady signal. Birds' bodies respond to it, and they also have a yearly clock inside them. 'The first cold day' is a common guess, but many birds leave while it is still warm.

activities.context: In this activity you draw the yearly journeys of three animals that pass through India: a falcon, a swallow and a butterfly.

flow.do: 1. Find one plant with flowers that open at a set time: a lotus, morning glory, pavazhamalli or four o'clock plant. 2. Visit early in the morning. 3. Draw the flowers and write the time.

flow.kid: Draw the flowers. Are they open or closed? Write the time.

flow.say: Same flowers, later in the day. What has changed?
flow.kid: Draw the same flowers again. What changed?

flow.say: Why might this flower open at that time, and not another?
flow.kid: Look at both drawings. Why does this flower open at that time?
flow.think: Who visits this flower? When do they come?

activities.title: A Swallow's Year: act it out

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper labelled 'North: summer', 'Flying south', 'India: winter', 'Flying north'
a torch, for the Sun

activities.safety: Clear a space so nobody trips.

schedule.what: Act out a barn swallow's year around four paper signs on the floor.

activities.record: Draw the four parts of the swallow's year in a circle.

flow.do: 1. Put the four sheets on the floor in a circle. 2. Your child is the swallow, standing on 'North: summer'. 3. A grown-up holds the torch high and steady, for long summer days.
flow.say: You are a barn swallow in the north in summer. The days are long and full of insects. Catch flies and feed your chicks.
flow.kid: You are a swallow. It is summer in the north. Long days. Lots of insects. Flap and catch flies!
flow.context: This is the first step of an act-out of a barn swallow's year. You move round four signs on the floor as the seasons change.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up lowers the torch and switches it off more often, for shorter days. 2. Your child eats more, then flies to 'Flying south', then to 'India: winter'.
flow.say: The days are getting shorter. Your body knows. You eat and eat, then you fly south, mostly at night.
flow.kid: The days get shorter. Eat lots! Now fly south. Land on the wires in India.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up makes the days long again. 2. Your child flies north. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Spring. The days grow longer. Back to the north, to nest.
flow.kid: The days get longer. Fly back north. Build a nest.

check.q: Why does the swallow fly back north in spring, when India still has food?
options: India gets too crowded with crows
Long northern summer days give many hours to catch insects for the chicks
check.why: In the far north, summer days are very long and insects are everywhere. Parents can feed chicks for many hours a day. 'Too crowded' is a guess that scientists have not shown.

activities.context: This is an act-out of one year in the life of a barn swallow, moving between the north and India as the days change. It is a demonstration, not an experiment.

projects.title: Our Window Calendar

materials.item: a notebook kept by one window or the balcony
a pencil and colours
binoculars, if you have them

projects.safety: Watch from inside the grille or balcony rail. Never lean out.

schedule.what: Set up the calendar. Write the date, sunset time and three living things you can see or hear.
Second entry, on the same day of the week, at the same time.
Third entry.
Last entry. Read all four, and write what changed and what stayed the same.

projects.record: Four dated entries, each with the time the streetlights came on and the living things seen or heard. A last page saying what changed.

flow.do: 1. Choose one window or the balcony. 2. Write the date and the time the streetlights come on. 3. Write three living things you can see or hear there: birds, flowers, trees, insects. 4. Draw one of them.
flow.say: Like Arjun's nature calendar, we'll write what this window shows us, once a week for four weeks.
flow.kid: Write today's date. What time did the streetlights come on? Write three living things you see or hear. Draw one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Window Calendar, a four-week project. You record the same window once a week, to see slow changes.

flow.do: Each week, on the same day and at the same time, write a new entry the same way.
flow.say: Same window, same time. What's new? What has gone?
flow.kid: Same window, same time. What is new this week? What has gone?
flow.wait: Come back next week, and the week after.

flow.do: After four weeks, read all the entries together.
flow.say: Did the streetlights come on earlier or later? Did any birds or flowers come or go?
flow.kid: Read all four entries. What changed? What stayed the same?

check.q: Over four weeks, the streetlights came on a little earlier each week. What does this tell you?
check.why: Streetlights switch on when it gets dark. If that happens earlier, sunset is earlier and the days are getting shorter. This is the same change birds and plants read. 'Broken' is a fair doubt, so check the sunset time in a newspaper or on a phone too.

projects.context: In this four-week project you keep a calendar of one window or balcony, writing down what changes, the way living things read the year.

challenges.problem: Most migrating birds fly at night. Bright lights on tall buildings pull them off their path, and they can crash into the glass. Design a way for a tall building in your city to help migrating birds, while people still work there.
constraints: People inside must still be able to see and work.
It must work during the migration months, when birds pass.
Draw it, and make a small model with a box and a torch.
materials: paper, tape, colour pencils, a dark cloth
general: Switch off or dim the outside lights and top-floor lights during the migration months, as some cities in America do.
Pull curtains or blinds at night, so less light shines out.
Put patterns of dots or lines on the glass, so birds see it is solid.
creative: Lamps that point down at the desk, not out of the window.
A calendar alarm that dims the building on the nights birds are expected.
A 'bird forecast': scientists already use weather radar to predict big migration nights.

flow.do: Draw three ideas together.
flow.say: How could the people inside still see, but less light get out?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. People still need to see. Less light should get out.

flow.do: 1. Add the best idea to the box. 2. Test it in the dark room. 3. Improve it and test again.
flow.say: Let's test it. Does less light escape?
flow.kid: Add your idea to the box. Test it in the dark. Better? Change it and try again.

flow.kid: Read what cities already do. Can you think of something new?
flow.think: Who else is harmed by bright light at night? Think of moths, turtles and people.
