quiz.p: Which of these is a yearly rhythm?
quiz.why: The konrai flowers once a year, around Vishu in April. The others happen every day.

quiz.p: Usha, a girl in Hyderabad, keeps a bean plant in a dark box overnight. In the morning, before she lets any light in, what does she most likely see?
opts: The leaves held out flat again
quiz.why: The plant's body clock lifts the leaves in the morning, even in the dark. Picking 'still hanging down' is the most common guess, because it seems the dark should keep the leaves down.

quiz.p: What resets a body clock each day?
quiz.why: Light in the morning sets the body clock right, so it does not drift. This is why jet lag wears off after a few days of daylight in a new place.

quiz.p: Why do many flowers open only at a certain time of day?
opts: To be open when their pollinators visit
Because the Sun tells each flower separately
quiz.why: Flowers need visitors such as bees and moths to carry pollen. Opening when the visitors come saves scent and nectar.

quiz.p: Why do many small birds leave the far north in autumn?
opts: Food such as insects runs out in winter
They are bored of the north
quiz.why: A small bird must eat many times a day. In winter, lakes freeze and insects vanish, so the birds fly to places like India where there is food.

quiz.p: What do many birds use to tell when it is time to migrate?
opts: The days getting shorter or longer
quiz.why: Day length changes the same way every year, so it is a reliable signal. Birds also have a yearly clock inside them.

quiz.p: Before 1822, many people in Europe thought swallows spent the winter where?
opts: Asleep in the mud at the bottom of lakes
quiz.why: Writers such as Olaus Magnus said swallows slept in mud. A stork found with an African spear in 1822 helped show that birds fly far away instead.

quiz.p: What do scientists still not agree on?
opts: Why some leaves droop at night
quiz.why: Scientists agree that leaves move and that plants have clocks. Why the drooping helps is still argued: keeping warm, keeping moonlight off, or staying dry.

quiz.p: Sevanthi plants on a balcony grow flower buds in November. What signal tells them it is time?
quiz.why: Sevanthi, the chrysanthemum, flowers when the nights grow long. This use of day length is called photoperiodism.

quiz.p: A body clock in steady darkness keeps going but slowly drifts. Why does it drift?
opts: It runs a little faster or slower than 24 hours
quiz.why: A body clock runs close to 24 hours, but not exactly. Without light to reset it, the small difference adds up each day.

quiz.p: Why does a bean plant gain from lifting their leaves before sunrise?
opts: They are ready to make food with the first light
quiz.why: Plants make food from light. A plant that is ready before the light comes wastes none of the morning.

quiz.p: Amur falcons rest in Nagaland in October. Where do they fly next?
opts: Across the Arabian Sea to southern Africa
quiz.why: After feeding in Nagaland, Amur falcons cross the Arabian Sea to spend the winter in southern Africa, then fly back in spring.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, looks at her bean plant at 9 at night. What will the first two leaves most likely be doing?
items.why: Bean leaves droop at night and are held flat in the day. This is called a sleep movement. A strong answer also says the leaves will lift again in the morning.

items.p: A daily rhythm is a change that happens about once every 24 hours.
items.why: True. Daily rhythms follow the Earth's spin, which brings light and dark about every 24 hours. Sleeping and waking is one.

items.p: Match each flower to the time it usually opens.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each flower opens when their visitors are about. A strong answer can name a visitor, such as bees by day or moths at night.

items.p: A timer inside a living thing that keeps a rhythm of about 24 hours is called a body ____.
items.why: A body clock keeps time even in steady darkness, like the bean plant in the box. Light resets it each morning.

items.p: In the bean test, why did we keep the box cup in the same room as the window cup?
items.a: So both cups were equally warm. Then the only difference between them was the light, so any difference in the leaves would come from the light.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of a fair test: change only one thing.

items.p: Sort these into daily rhythms and yearly rhythms.
items: Bean leaves hanging down at night
Swallows coming to India for winter
Sevanthi flowering when nights grow long
items.a: see items
items.why: Daily rhythms repeat each day, with light and dark. Yearly rhythms repeat each year, with the seasons. A strong answer can say what sets each one.

items.p: Barn swallows sit on the electric wires in Chennai in January. Where are they most likely to be in June?
opts: Asleep in mud under a lake
Far to the north, raising chicks
items.why: Barn swallows spend the winter in India and fly north in spring to nest. 'Asleep in mud' was what people believed for centuries, until the evidence showed it was wrong.

items.p: Draw a bean plant at noon and the same plant at 9 at night. Label the leaves 'flat' or 'hanging down'.
items.a: Two drawings: at noon the two leaves held out flat, at night the leaves hanging down close to the stem.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the stem the same in both, with only the leaves changed. A small joint at the base of each leaf, the pulvinus, does the bending.
items.art: Two empty boxes labelled 'noon' and '9 at night'.

items.p: Three of these are about migration. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Butterflies flying to the Western Ghats
A bean leaf drooping at night
items.why: A drooping bean leaf is a daily rhythm in one place. The others are long yearly journeys, which is migration.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi talk about why birds fly south for winter.

views.says: Birds fly south because they feel cold. The cold tells them to go.
Birds fly south because the food runs out. Frozen lakes and no insects mean nothing to eat.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that food is the main problem, because a small bird must eat often to stay warm, and winter takes the food away. Many birds also leave while it is still warm, as the days shorten. But Divya is right that cold is part of the story: the cold is what freezes the lakes and kills the insects.
items.why: Both views hold something true. A strong answer links cold, food and day length.

items.p: Put the steps of the bean test in order.
items: Put one cup under a dark box in the evening
Plant soaked rajma seeds in two cups
Peek into the box the next morning
Wait for the first two leaves to open
a: Plant soaked rajma seeds in two cups
Wait for the first two leaves to open
Put one cup under a dark box in the evening
Peek into the box the next morning
items.why: First grow the plants, then wait until they have leaves to watch, then start the test, then check.

items.p: Lakshmi says, 'Plants only move their leaves when someone touches them.' Is she right?
items.why: False. Bean, tamarind and rain tree leaves move every evening and morning with no touch at all. Touch-me-not also folds when touched, but that is a different movement.

items.p: Your body is coolest early in the morning and warmest in the late afternoon. Why did we measure on three days, not one?
items.a: One reading can be a fluke. A thermometer reading can jump by a little, or I might have just run about. Three days show whether the pattern really repeats.
items.why: A strong answer says that repeating a test shows whether a result is real.

items.p: Why does a jasmine flower give out the most smell in the evening and night?
opts: The smell is stronger in the dark
Their visitors, such as moths, come then
People are home in the evening
items.why: Smell guides visitors to the flower. Many white night flowers are visited by moths, which fly at night. Making scent when nobody is coming would waste it. 'People are home' is about us, not the flower's visitors.

items.p: Label the parts of this bean seedling: stem, leaf, pulvinus (the leaf joint), root.
items.why: The pulvinus is the small swollen joint where the leaf blade meets their stalk. Water moving in and out of its cells bends it, which lifts or lowers the leaf.
items.art: A bean seedling in a cup with four blank label lines pointing to the stem, a leaf, the small joint at the leaf base, and the roots.

items.p: Name one daily rhythm in your own body, and say when it happens.
items.a: For example: I feel sleepy at about 9 at night, or I feel hungry at about 1 in the afternoon, or my body is coolest in the early morning.
items.why: A strong answer gives a time, and notices it happens about the same time each day.

items.p: Kavya puts her bean plant in a dark cupboard for two days. Their leaves still lift each morning and droop each night. What sets the timing?
opts: The plant's roots seeing the soil
A body clock inside the plant
items.why: No light reached the plant, so the timing came from inside them, from their body clock. A strong answer adds that the days on the windowsill had set that clock before.

items.p: A body clock runs a little fast or slow. What would happen to a plant's clock if the plant stayed in the dark for many weeks?
items.a: The clock would drift away from the real day, a little more each day. After many days the leaves would lift at the wrong time. The plant would also run out of food, because they cannot make food without light.
items.why: A strong answer explains that light resets the clock each morning, so without light the clock slowly drifts.

items.p: Three people look at a bean plant whose leaves rose in a dark box.

views.says: The plant knows it is morning. They measure time and get ready for the light.
It is just chemistry. Substances build up and break down in a loop, and that moves the leaf.
Both are true. Knowing the time can be made of chemistry, like my own body clock.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give your reason, using what you saw in the bean test. Then say what one of the other views gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the evidence: the leaves rose before any light came, so the plant was timing the change from inside. It can say that the plant senses and acts on time, and also that the clock is made of genes and chemistry. It treats each view fairly.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about words like 'know' and 'decide'. There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses evidence and is fair to the others.

items.p: The way living things use the length of the day to tell the season is called ____.
items.why: 'Photo' means light and 'period' means a length of time. Sevanthi uses it to flower when the nights grow long.

items.p: Sort each change by what sets its timing.
cats: Day length or a body clock
items: Day length or a body clock
Day length or a body clock
Frogs calling at the start of the monsoon
Day length or a body clock
items.a: see items
items.why: Signs set by day length or a clock come at nearly the same date every year. Signs set by rain come on a different date each year, depending on when the rain comes.

items.p: In Srinagar, day length changes by about 4 and a half hours across the year. In Chennai, it changes by only about 1 and a half hours. Where would day length be the easiest signal of the season?
items.why: A bigger change is easier to notice. Further from the equator, day length changes more over the year. Near the equator, many living things use rain more than day length.

items.p: Draw a circle for one year. Mark when barn swallows are in India and when they are in the north. Add what they do in each place.
items.a: A circle with the cold months, about October to March, labelled 'India: feeding', and the warm months labelled 'North: nesting and raising chicks', with arrows for the journeys between.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the year as a loop that repeats, with a reason for each half.
items.art: An empty circle with the months written round the edge.

items.p: Eberhard Gwinner kept warblers in a room where the light stayed the same all year. They still became restless at about migration time.
items.why: True. The birds have a yearly clock inside them. In the steady room it ran about 10 months, not 12, so in the wild, day length keeps it on time.

items.p: Malli buds kept inside a closed dabba opened at nearly the same time as buds on an open plate. What would that tell you?
items.a: That the buds did not need to see the evening to open. The timing came from inside them, from a clock, set by the days before.
items.why: A strong answer reasons from evidence. It might also say that if the dabba buds opened later, the evening light would be part of the signal.

items.p: Put a migrating bird's autumn in order.
items: Arrive in India and find food
Eat a lot and store fat
a: Eat a lot and store fat
Arrive in India and find food
items.why: The change in day length comes first. It changes the bird's body, so they eat and store fat for fuel. Then they fly.

items.p: Why is it useful for a plant to start lifting their leaves before sunrise?
opts: They can use the very first light to make food
items.why: Plants make food from light, air and water. Being ready before the light comes means no morning light is wasted. Plants whose clocks match the day grow better.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: travel far at the same time each year
rest deeply through the cold season
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words describe how animals fit their lives to the day and the year.

items.p: Two sisters in Mysuru talk about how the swallows know when to come to India.

views.says: The swallows learn it from older swallows, by flying with them.
The swallows are born knowing. Something inside them tells them when.

items.ask: Which sister do you think is closer to the truth? Use the warbler experiment in your answer. Then say what the other sister might have right.
items.a: A strong answer uses Gwinner's warblers, which became restless at migration time in a closed room, so the timing is inside them, as Revathi says. It also gives Nila her due: many birds fly in flocks, and some learn the route from others. Timing and route might be learned in different ways.
items.why: Scientists think the timing comes mostly from inside, set by day length, while finding the way uses inborn sense and learning together.

items.p: City lights are bright all night. Explain one way this could harm a migrating bird.
items.a: Birds that fly at night can be pulled towards bright lights. They may circle until they are tired, or crash into the glass of a lit building.
items.why: A strong answer links night flight to light at night.

items.p: Three of these flowers usually open in the evening or at night. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: The lotus opens in the early morning. Jasmine opens in the evening, and pavazhamalli and Brahma kamal open at night.

items.p: On this map, label: the place Amur falcons start, the place they rest in India, and the place they spend the winter.
items.why: Amur falcons nest in eastern China and Russia, rest and feed in Nagaland in October and November, and fly across the Arabian Sea to winter in southern Africa.
items.art: An outline map of Asia, the Arabian Sea and Africa with three blank label boxes and a dotted path between them.

items.p: In the bean test, the box cup's leaves rose on the first morning, but on the second morning only half way. Suggest a reason.
items.a: Without light, the plant's clock was not reset, so it may have started to drift. Or the plant was getting weaker without light to make food. A third reason could be that peeking let a little light in at the wrong time.
items.why: A strong answer gives more than one possible reason and says how to test one of them.

items.p: Three scientists argue about why bean leaves droop at night.

views.says: Drooping leaves lose less warmth to the cold night sky.
Drooping leaves keep moonlight off, so it cannot confuse the plant's clock.
Drooping leaves stay drier, so fewer fungi grow on them.

items.ask: Choose the idea you think is most likely. Describe a test you could do at home or in a lab to check it. Then say what the other ideas have going for them.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and designs a fair test: for example, pin some leaves open and compare them on cold nights with leaves left free, as Darwin did. It says that nobody yet knows for sure, and that more than one reason may be true.
items.why: This is a real open question. Scientists have evidence for several ideas. A strong answer designs a test that changes only one thing.

items.p: Arjun's grandmother says, 'The eesal come out after the first big rain.' This year the rain came a month late. When did the eesal come?
opts: On the same date as last year
Before the rain, as a warning
items.why: Winged termites fly out after heavy rain softens the ground. So they follow the rain, not the date. Signs set by day length come on nearly the same date each year. Signs set by rain move with the rain.

items.p: A plant whose clock matches the length of the day grows bigger than one whose clock does not. Explain why, in your own words.
items.a: A plant with a matching clock is ready at the right times. Their leaves are up and their food-making parts are ready before dawn, so they use all the light. A plant with a wrong clock is ready too early or too late, so they waste some light.
items.why: A strong answer links getting ready early with using every hour of light.

items.p: Draw a graph of how warm your body is across one day, from waking to bedtime. Use your own results if you did the warm and cool test.
items.a: A line that starts lowest at waking, rises through the day to the highest point in the late afternoon or early evening, and falls a little by bedtime.
items.why: A strong graph has the times along the bottom and temperatures up the side, and shows a smooth rise and fall.
items.art: Empty axes: time of day along the bottom, temperature in degrees up the side.

items.p: On the Great Barrier Reef, many corals release their eggs on the same few nights each year, after a full moon. Why does this help them?
opts: The Moon pulls the eggs up to the surface
Eggs and sperm from many corals meet in the water at once
items.why: Corals cannot move to find each other. If they all release at once, their eggs and sperm meet. The Moon is a clock they share. 'The Moon pulls the eggs up' mixes this up with tides.

items.p: In 2021, the cherry trees of Kyoto, in Japan, flowered earlier than at any time in more than 1,200 years of records. Why might early flowers be a problem for bees?
items.a: If the flowers open before the bees are active, the bees miss the nectar and the flowers miss being pollinated. The flowers and bees keep different clocks, so warming can put them out of step.
items.why: A strong answer explains that two living things must stay in step, and a change can affect one more than the other.

items.p: Day length is a steadier signal of the season than warmth.
items.why: True. One hot week in January cannot change day length, which follows the Earth's path round the Sun. That is why many plants and birds use it.

items.p: Teenagers' body clocks run later than younger children's. Should schools for teenagers start later? Give one reason for and one against.
items.a: For: teenagers would sleep more and learn better in the morning. Against: parents' work times, buses and sports may not fit, and families would need to change their whole day.
items.why: A strong answer uses the science of body clocks for one side and real-life trade-offs for the other. Some schools in other countries have tried later starts.

items.p: Sort these by what the living thing keeps time with.
items: Grunion fish laying eggs on beaches
items.a: see items
items.why: Living things keep time with the Earth's spin, the Moon's cycle and the year. A strong answer can give the problem each rhythm solves.

items.p: In 1822 a stork was found in Germany with a spear from Africa in their neck. Why did this change people's minds?
opts: It showed the stork had been in Africa and flown back
It showed storks like Africa better
items.why: The spear was African, so the stork must have been in Africa. That ruled out the old idea that birds slept in mud all winter. One clear piece of evidence can overturn a belief held for centuries.

items.p: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Hans Christian Mortensen began putting rings on birds
Olaus Magnus wrote that swallows sleep in mud
Aristotle wrote that some birds hide in winter
A stork with an African spear was found in Germany
a: Aristotle wrote that some birds hide in winter
Olaus Magnus wrote that swallows sleep in mud
A stork with an African spear was found in Germany
Hans Christian Mortensen began putting rings on birds
items.why: Aristotle lived over 2,300 years ago, Olaus Magnus wrote in 1555, the stork was found in 1822, and ringing began in 1899.

items.p: Many people think plants only react: light comes, then the leaves open. What from this unit challenges that idea?
items.a: In the dark box, bean leaves lifted in the morning before any light could reach them. A reaction comes after the thing it reacts to. These leaves moved with no light at all, so the plant was keeping time and getting ready.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence from the bean test to argue against a popular belief.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether malli buds need warmth to open on time. Draw the setup and label what stays the same.
items.a: Two groups of buds from one string, both in the dark, one in a cool place such as near a window at night and one in a warmer place. Same number of buds, same damp cloth, same times for counting.
items.why: A strong design changes only the warmth and keeps the light, buds, water and timing the same. A fridge is too cold and would harm the buds.
items.art: An empty box for a drawing.

items.p: Michael, a night-shift nurse, works all night and sleeps by day. He often feels sleepy at work. What is the best explanation?
opts: His body clock still expects him to sleep at night
items.why: The body clock is set by daylight, so it keeps telling his body that night is for sleep. Bright light at work and dark curtains at home can help shift it.

items.p: Living things get ready for sunrise before it comes. Name two things in your family's day that are done to be ready before something happens.
items.a: For example: soaking rice and dal at night so the idli batter is ready by morning, or setting out school clothes the night before.
items.why: A strong answer sees the same pattern as the bean plant: preparing ahead saves time when the moment comes.

applications: Doctors give some medicines at the time of day they work best, because the body changes through the day.
Night-shift workers, pilots and astronauts use bright light and dark rooms to shift their body clocks.
Farmers choose rice and other crop varieties that flower at the right time of year for their region.
Flower growers use extra light at night to make chrysanthemums flower later.
Cities dim building lights during the bird migration months.
Bird scientists use rings and tiny trackers to follow migrations and protect resting places such as Nagaland's Doyang reservoir.
Weather radar is used to forecast big nights of bird migration.
Fishers in many places time their work by the tides and the Moon.
Sleep doctors help people whose body clocks run too early or too late.

open_questions.q: Why do some leaves droop or fold at night?
open_questions.why_open: Keeping warm, keeping moonlight off and staying dry all have some evidence. Nobody has shown which matters most, or whether it differs between plants.

open_questions.q: How do all the clocks in one body stay in step?
open_questions.why_open: Almost every cell has a clock. Scientists know the main clock genes, but how the clocks of leaves, roots or organs talk to each other is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How does a young bird know where to go on their first migration?
open_questions.why_open: Some young birds fly alone to places they have never seen. Scientists think the direction is inborn, but how it is stored is not known.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do birds sense the Earth's magnetic field to find their way?
open_questions.why_open: The leading idea involves a substance in their eyes. It has strong evidence but is not fully proven in wild birds.

open_questions.q: How do corals sense the moonlight so exactly?
open_questions.why_open: Corals have no eyes, but have light-sensing substances. How they count the nights after a full moon is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How will a warming world change nature's calendar?
open_questions.why_open: Some plants and animals are shifting their timing and some are not. Scientists are watching which ones fall out of step, and what happens then.

maths.problem: In the warm and cool test, Kavya's temperature was 36.3 °C just after waking and 36.8 °C at 5 pm. How much warmer was she at 5 pm?
maths.answer: 0.5 °C warmer, which is half a degree.
maths.explain: 36.8 take away 36.3 is 0.5. Think of it as 368 tenths take away 363 tenths, which is 5 tenths. Half a degree is small, but it came back on every day she measured.
maths.context: This is about the warm and cool test, where you measure your body's temperature at three times of day.
maths.why_maths: A rhythm is a pattern of change. Taking one reading from another tells us how big the change is.

maths.problem: In Chennai, the longest day is about 12 hours 55 minutes and the shortest is about 11 hours 20 minutes. In Srinagar, they are about 14 hours 25 minutes and 9 hours 55 minutes. In which city does day length change more across the year, and by how much?
maths.answer: Srinagar. Day length changes by about 4 hours 30 minutes there, and by about 1 hour 35 minutes in Chennai.
maths.explain: Chennai: 12 hours 55 minutes take away 11 hours 20 minutes is 1 hour 35 minutes. Srinagar: 14 hours 25 minutes take away 9 hours 55 minutes. From 9 hours 55 minutes to 10 hours is 5 minutes, then 4 hours 25 minutes more to 14 hours 25 minutes. Total 4 hours 30 minutes. That is nearly three times as much change as in Chennai.
maths.context: Day length is the time from sunrise to sunset. It changes through the year, and it changes more in the north of India.

chart.title: Change in day length across the year

maths.show: Two clock faces for each city, one for the longest day and one for the shortest, with the daylight shaded.
maths.why_maths: Birds and plants read day length. Working out how much it changes shows why it is a stronger signal in the north than near the equator.

maths.problem: In the malli buds test, 7 of the 10 buds on the plate were open at 8 pm, and 6 of the 10 buds in the dabba were open. Is that a big difference, or nearly the same? What would you do to be more sure?
maths.answer: Nearly the same: only 1 bud different out of 10. To be more sure, repeat with more buds, or on another evening.
maths.explain: 7 and 6 differ by 1. With only 10 buds, one bud that was a little slow could make that difference by chance. If the dabba had 1 open and the plate 7, that would be a big difference. Repeating the test shows whether a small difference is real.
maths.context: This is about the malli buds test, where you count how many jasmine buds have opened on an open plate and in a closed dabba.
maths.why_maths: Scientists must decide whether a difference is real or just chance. Comparing the size of the difference with the number tested helps.

maths.problem: Amur falcons cross about 4,000 kilometres of sea without stopping. If they fly about 1,000 kilometres a day, how many days and nights are they over the sea?
maths.explain: 4,000 divided by 1,000 is 4. Check: 1,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 = 4,000. The falcons cannot land on water, so they must store enough fat before they leave to last all 4 days.
maths.context: Amur falcons rest in Nagaland and then cross the Arabian Sea to Africa. This problem works out how long the sea crossing takes.
maths.show: A map with a dotted line from India across the sea to Africa, split into four equal parts with a small sun over each.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the distance by the distance per day tells us how long the birds must fly without food, which explains why they store fat first.

maths.problem: In the bean test, Riya gave each leaf position a number: flat is 2, half down is 1, hanging down is 0. Her window cup scored 2 at 7 am, 2 at 1 pm, 1 at 6 pm and 0 at 9 pm. Draw these as a line graph. What do you predict for 7 am the next day?
maths.answer: A line that stays high in the morning and afternoon, then falls in the evening to 0 at night. The next morning should be 2 again.
maths.explain: A line graph shows change over time. The line is flat at 2 in the day, drops to 1 at 6 pm and to 0 at 9 pm. Because the leaves move on a daily rhythm, the pattern repeats, so at 7 am the next day the score should be back to 2.
maths.context: This is about the sleeping bean leaves test, where you check the leaves at four times of day.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows a rhythm as a shape. Once you see the shape, you can predict what comes next.

roots.context: We have watched bean leaves rise and fall, jasmine open in the evening and swallows come for the winter. Now we ask what nature's clocks tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the dark box, your bean plant still lifted their leaves in the morning. No light reached them, so the timing came from inside the plant. Earlier days on the windowsill had set that inside clock. So a plant expects the morning, and gets ready before it comes.
deep_truth.habit: We think of plants as only reacting: light comes, then leaves open. But a reaction comes after its cause. Your plant moved before any light came, so they were expecting the day, not answering it.
deep_truth.evidence: The box cup's leaves were flat in the morning and hanging down at night, like the window cup, with no light at all. Taken out of the box, they kept going on the window's rhythm.

three.who_am_i: You have a body clock too. It cools you before dawn and warms you through the day, without asking you.
three.what_is_life: Living things keep time. Leaves, flowers, falcons and corals all get ready for what is coming.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth spins once a day and goes round the Sun once a year. Every living thing on it has learned those two beats.

roots.thread: The Earth makes one rhythm: one spin a day, one trip round the Sun a year. From that one rhythm come countless clocks. The bean lifts their leaves, the jasmine opens at evening, the swallow leaves the north, the coral waits for the moon, and you wake up. Each keeps their own time, yet all of them follow the same turning Earth.

science.text: Plants, animals, fungi and many bacteria have body clocks of about 24 hours, made by genes in a loop. Light resets them each day.
Plants feel the length of the night and use it to decide when to flower. Some scientists call this an automatic response.
How the many clocks in one body stay in step is not fully known.

other_view.view: A plant's clock is a loop of genes and chemicals, as steady as a ticking wall clock. Saying the plant 'expects' the morning adds a feeling that the experiment cannot show. They would say the plant is timed, not expecting.

practice.title: Guess the time with your body

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Kitchen rajma usually sprouts, so the bean test uses 6 seeds in two cups and says what to do if none come up. The first two leaves take about 8 to 12 days, so the test waits for them before the checks start. The dark box stays in the same room, so only the light changes. Peeks last a few seconds. Room lights late at night can confuse the night check, so the step says to check in a dim corner. The warm and cool test uses only a digital thermometer, measures after sitting still for 15 minutes, and repeats for three days, because a single reading can jump. Underarm readings vary more, and the step says no pattern is honest data too. The malli test uses buds bought in the afternoon. We found no study on whether jasmine buds open on time in darkness, so the step tells parents that either result is real. The Moon, tide and coral rhythms are taught on cards, not tested. Both games work for one child alone. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes, though the bean test is spread over about 12 days.

how_we_found_out.story: Every autumn in Europe, storks and swallows disappeared, and every spring they came back. For about 2,000 years, people argued about where they went. The Greek thinker Aristotle wrote that some birds hid and slept through the winter. In 1555, the Swedish writer Olaus Magnus wrote that swallows sank into lakes and slept in the mud until spring. Many people believed this for the next 250 years. Then, in 1822, a white stork was shot near the village of Klütz, in northern Germany. Through the stork's neck was a long wooden spear, about 75 centimetres long. The spear was not from Germany. It was the kind made in central Africa. The stork had been speared in Africa in the winter, survived, and flown thousands of kilometres back with it. So the birds had not slept in mud. They had flown to Africa. Later, about 25 more storks with African arrows were found in Germany. In 1899, the Danish teacher Hans Christian Mortensen began putting numbered rings on birds' legs. Rings found in faraway places showed the journeys clearly.
how_we_found_out.who: The people of Klütz and the scientists at the University of Rostock, who still keep the stork, and Hans Christian Mortensen, a Danish teacher who began ringing birds
how_we_found_out.when: 1822 (the stork with the spear) and 1899 (the first numbered bird rings)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought swallows and other birds spent the winter asleep, hidden or in the mud at the bottom of lakes. The stork with an African spear in their neck showed that birds fly to Africa for the winter and come back.
